client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away last month. Everything just feels kind of gray and hollow — like I go through the motions of my day but nothing actually feels good or meaningful anymore. I'm not even sure talking about it will change anything, but I figured I had to try something because I can't keep feeling this way.
therapist: What you're carrying right now — the grief, that hollow feeling, going through the days without anything really landing — that makes complete sense after losing someone so important to you. I'm really glad you decided to reach out, and I want you to know that even just putting words to this experience is a meaningful first step. Can you tell me a little more about what your grandmother meant to you, and what life has looked like in the days since she passed?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: She was honestly the one person in my life who made me feel like I didn't have to explain myself, you know? I could just show up at her house and she'd make tea and we'd sit together and it didn't have to be anything — it just felt safe. Since she passed, I've been going to work, coming home, eating whatever's in the fridge, and just kind of staring at my phone until I fall asleep, and that's pretty much every day.
therapist: What you're describing about your grandmother is so tender — that rare kind of presence where you could just *be*, without performing or explaining yourself, is something truly irreplaceable. The way you're moving through your days right now — work, home, phone, sleep — it sounds less like living and more like waiting, like part of you is still paused at her loss. I'm wondering, when you're lying there at night staring at your phone, what's actually going through your mind in those quiet moments?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, a lot of the time I'm just scrolling mindlessly, but when I actually stop and let myself think, I keep going over the last few weeks before she died and wondering if I visited enough, if I said the right things, if she knew how much she meant to me. There's this nagging feeling that I let her down somehow, even though logically I know I was there pretty regularly — it just doesn't feel like enough. And then I'll think about calling someone to talk about it, but it feels pointless because nobody else really knew her the way I did, so what's the point.
therapist: That guilt you're describing — replaying those last weeks, wondering if it was enough — is such a common and painful part of grief, and it often hits hardest with the people who actually *cared the most*. The fact that you were there regularly and still feel like it wasn't enough tells me something important: your love for her was bigger than any number of visits could ever fully express, and that's not a failure — that's just how profound she was to you. I'm curious, if your grandmother were sitting with you right now, what do you think she would say about how you showed up for her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I know she would probably tell me I was a good grandchild and that she knew I loved her — she was always saying things like that, reassuring people. But when I try to actually picture her saying it to me right now, it feels kind of hollow, like I'm just putting words in her mouth because that's what I want to hear, not because it's fixing anything. I don't know, maybe I'm being too cynical, but I'm not sure imagining what she'd say really changes how I feel inside.
therapist: You're not being cynical at all — you're being honest, and that actually takes courage. It sounds like part of you *knows* she loved you and believed in you, but knowing something and *feeling* it in your body are two very different things right now, and grief has a way of creating that gap. I'm wondering — are there any specific memories, maybe a moment or something she actually said to you, that felt real and true in a way that still carries some weight for you today?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: There's this one moment I keep coming back to — maybe two years ago, I was going through a really rough patch at work and I showed up at her place kind of a mess, and she just looked at me and said "you're stronger than you think you are, and I've always known that." It felt real in a way that's hard to describe, like she was seeing something in me I couldn't see myself. But even thinking about it now, it mostly just makes me sad because that voice is gone, and I don't have anyone else in my life who sees me that way.
therapist: That moment you're describing is so vivid and real — and the fact that it stays with you so clearly tells me it landed deeply, that some part of you received what she saw in you, even if it's hard to hold onto right now. There's something tender in the way you shared that, and I notice that alongside the sadness, there might also be something quietly precious about still carrying her words with you. I'm wondering — when she said "you're stronger than you think you are," do you have any sense of what she was seeing in you that you still have trouble seeing in yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think she saw someone who kept going even when things were hard, like she'd watched me navigate enough difficult stuff over the years that she had this longer view of me than I have of myself. But honestly, right now I mostly feel like I'm just going through the motions rather than actually being strong — like whatever she saw might have been true then but I'm not sure it still applies. And I guess part of what scares me is that without her there to reflect that back to me, I don't really know how to hold onto it.
therapist: What you just described — that she held a longer view of you than you hold of yourself — is really profound, and I think it points to something important: that strength she saw wasn't something she *created*, it was something she *witnessed*, which means it belongs to you. Going through the motions right now isn't the absence of strength, it might actually be exactly what strength looks like in the middle of grief. I'm curious — if you tried to borrow her longer view for just a moment, what difficult things have you navigated over the years that she might have been quietly noting?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean, there have been things — a bad breakup a few years back that really knocked me down, losing a job once and having to start over, some health stuff with my dad that I basically managed mostly on my own. I can list them, but it feels a bit like I'm just reciting facts about someone else's life rather than actually feeling like those things say anything meaningful about who I am. I guess I'm skeptical that looking backwards at hard times I survived is going to fill that hole that's there now — it feels like a different kind of problem.
therapist: You've actually named something really important — those experiences are real, but right now they feel like they belong to a stranger, and that disconnection makes sense because grief can make us feel cut off from our own story. You're right that this isn't just about building confidence from past wins — the hole you're describing is about losing the one person who held your story *with* you and made it feel meaningful. I'm wondering, is part of what hurts not just losing her presence, but also feeling like you lost the one witness to who you really are?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I think that's actually exactly it — and hearing you say it out loud kind of hit me harder than I expected. It's not just that she's gone, it's that the person who knew the whole story, who remembered things about me I've half forgotten, isn't there anymore, and that feels like a specific kind of loneliness I don't know how to explain to anyone else. And I guess that's also why the idea of talking to friends or family about this feels so useless — they only have pieces of me, not the whole picture the way she did.
therapist: What you just put into words — that specific loneliness of losing your witness — is something really profound, and I can hear that it landed somewhere deep even as you said it. I notice you're speaking about something that feels so heavy, but there's something almost quiet and contained in how you're holding it right now, like maybe the weight of it is sitting heavier inside than what's coming out. I'm wondering — what does it feel like in your body as you sit with that realization?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: There's this kind of heaviness in my chest, like something is sitting on it that won't move, and my throat feels tight in a way that makes me want to just stop talking and go quiet. I don't usually pay attention to that stuff — I tend to just push through it and keep functioning — so it's a little uncomfortable to actually notice it right now. I'm not sure what I'm supposed to do with that feeling even if I can identify it.
therapist: The fact that you can notice that heaviness and tightness right now, even though it's uncomfortable, is actually really significant — you're not just pushing through for once, you're pausing to actually be with yourself. You don't have to *do* anything with that feeling right now; sometimes just letting it be there without running from it is enough, and that itself is a form of the strength your grandmother saw in you. What would it feel like to just sit with it for a moment, rather than needing to solve or explain it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, sitting with it without trying to fix it or explain it feels kind of terrifying, because the moment I stop trying to manage it I'm worried it'll just swallow me whole. I think I've spent a lot of years treating feelings like problems to solve, so just letting something be there without a plan feels really foreign and maybe a little pointless. I want to believe that's enough, but part of me keeps asking — then what, you know?
therapist: That fear of being swallowed whole makes so much sense, especially when managing and solving has been your armor for so long — it's kept you functioning through a lot of hard things, so of course letting go of it even briefly feels dangerous. But I want to gently offer this: the fact that you've carried this much grief for a month and it *hasn't* swallowed you, even while you've been pushing through alone, suggests you may be more able to bear it than you're giving yourself credit for. What do you think it would take — even just a small thing — to feel safe enough to let yourself feel it without needing to have the "then what" answered first?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
